raw: {"refusal": null, "claims": [{"text": "Subject to DISP 1.6.2AR (which applies to EMD and PSD complaints), a respondent must, by the end of eight weeks after receiving the complaint, send the complainant either a 'final response' or a written response explaining why it cannot yet give a final response.", "cites": ["DISP 1.6.2"]}, {"text": "A 'final response' is a written response that accepts the complaint (offering redress or remedial action where appropriate), or offers redress or remedial action without accepting the complaint, or rejects the complaint and gives reasons.", "cites": ["DISP 1.6.2"]}, {"text": "A final response must also enclose a copy of the Financial Ombudsman Service's standard explanatory leaflet, provide the FOS website address, inform the complainant that they may now refer the complaint to the FOS if still dissatisfied, and indicate whether the respondent consents to waive the relevant time limits in DISP 2.8.2 R or DISP 2.8.7 R.", "cites": ["DISP 1.6.2"]}, {"text": "The alternative written response must explain why the respondent cannot make a final response and indicate when it expects to be able to provide one, inform the complainant that they may now refer the complaint to the FOS, indicate whether the respondent consents to waive the relevant time limits if the complaint turns out to be outside them, enclose the FOS standard explanatory leaflet, and provide the FOS website address.", "cites": ["DISP 1.6.2"]}]}

claims.text: Subject to DISP 1.6.2AR (which applies to EMD and PSD complaints), a respondent must, by the end of eight weeks after receiving the complaint, send the complainant either a 'final response' or a written response explaining why it cannot yet give a final response.

A 'final response' is a written response that accepts the complaint (offering redress or remedial action where appropriate), or offers redress or remedial action without accepting the complaint, or rejects the complaint and gives reasons.

A final response must also enclose a copy of the Financial Ombudsman Service's standard explanatory leaflet, provide the FOS website address, inform the complainant that they may now refer the complaint to the FOS if still dissatisfied, and indicate whether the respondent consents to waive the relevant time limits in DISP 2.8.2 R or DISP 2.8.7 R.

The alternative written response must explain why the respondent cannot make a final response and indicate when it expects to be able to provide one, inform the complainant that they may now refer the complaint to the FOS, indicate whether the respondent consents to waive the relevant time limits if the complaint turns out to be outside them, enclose the FOS standard explanatory leaflet, and provide the FOS website address.

claims.text: A firm must design and deliver customer support so that retail customers do not face unreasonable barriers (including unreasonable additional costs) during the product lifecycle, including when they want to cancel a contract, agreement or arrangement or otherwise terminate their relationship with the firm.

Unreasonable barriers include steps that are likely to cause customers to take unreasonable additional steps, such as steps that are unreasonably onerous or time consuming, complex to carry out, or difficult to understand, and asking customers for unnecessary information or evidence.
Unreasonable additional costs include unreasonable exit fees or other charges, delays, distress or inconvenience.

Appropriate friction that a firm has included in its customer journeys to mitigate the risk of harm and give customers sufficient opportunity to understand and assess their options would not amount to an unreasonable barrier.

A firm would be unlikely to meet its obligations if its support causes or is likely to cause disproportionately longer call waiting times to cancel or make changes to an existing product than to purchase a new product, or unreasonable delays in requesting or processing necessary information or evidence from customers.

raw: {"refusal": null, "claims": [{"text": "The passages do not set out a full list of complaints procedures a firm must have. They say only that summary details of internal complaints handling procedures should cover at least how the respondent fulfils its obligation to handle and seek to resolve relevant complaints and, where the complaint falls within the Financial Ombudsman Service's jurisdiction, that an unresolved complainant may be entitled to refer it to the Ombudsman.", "cites": ["DISP 1.2.3"]}, {"text": "A respondent must put in place appropriate management controls and take reasonable steps to ensure that, in handling complaints, it identifies and remedies any recurring or systemic problems.", "cites": ["DISP 1.3.3"]}, {"text": "Examples of how to do this are analysing the causes of individual complaints to identify common root causes, considering whether those root causes may also affect other processes or products (including those not complained of), and correcting root causes where reasonable to do so.", "cites": ["DISP 1.3.3"]}, {"text": "Where a firm identifies recurring or systemic problems, it should consider whether it ought to act regarding customers who may have suffered detriment but have not complained, and if so take appropriate and proportionate measures to ensure they are given appropriate redress or a proper opportunity to obtain it.", "cites": ["DISP 1.3.6"]}, {"text": "In doing so, the firm should ascertain the scope and severity of the consumer detriment that might have arisen, and consider whether it is fair and reasonable to proactively undertake a redress or remediation exercise, which may include contacting customers who have not complained.", "cites": ["DISP 1.3.6"]}, {"text": "If a firm identifies, through complaints, internal monitoring or any other source, that retail customers have suffered foreseeable harm as a result of its acts or omissions, it must act in good faith and take appropriate action to rectify the situation, including providing redress where appropriate.", "cites": ["PRIN 2A.2.5"]}]}

claims.text: The passages do not set out a full list of complaints procedures a firm must have. They say only that summary details of internal complaints handling procedures should cover at least how the respondent fulfils its obligation to handle and seek to resolve relevant complaints and, where the complaint falls within the Financial Ombudsman Service's jurisdiction, that an unresolved complainant may be entitled to refer it to the Ombudsman.
A respondent must put in place appropriate management controls and take reasonable steps to ensure that, in handling complaints, it identifies and remedies any recurring or systemic problems.

Examples of how to do this are analysing the causes of individual complaints to identify common root causes, considering whether those root causes may also affect other processes or products (including those not complained of), and correcting root causes where reasonable to do so.

Where a firm identifies recurring or systemic problems, it should consider whether it ought to act regarding customers who may have suffered detriment but have not complained, and if so take appropriate and proportionate measures to ensure they are given appropriate redress or a proper opportunity to obtain it.

In doing so, the firm should ascertain the scope and severity of the consumer detriment that might have arisen, and consider whether it is fair and reasonable to proactively undertake a redress or remediation exercise, which may include contacting customers who have not complained.

If a firm identifies, through complaints, internal monitoring or any other source, that retail customers have suffered foreseeable harm as a result of its acts or omissions, it must act in good faith and take appropriate action to rectify the situation, including providing redress where appropriate.

claims.text: A firm must prepare a report for its governing body setting out the results of its monitoring under PRIN 2A.9 and any actions required as a result of that monitoring.
At least annually, the governing body must review and approve the firm's report on the outcomes being received by retail customers.

At least annually, the governing body must also confirm whether it is satisfied that the firm is complying with its obligations under the Consumer Duty, and assess whether the firm's future business strategy is consistent with those obligations.

When approving the report, the governing body must also agree any action required to address any identified risk that retail customers may not receive good outcomes, and any action required to address any identified instance where retail customers have not received good outcomes.
When approving the report, the governing body must also agree any amendments to the firm's business strategy needed to ensure it remains consistent with meeting the firm's Consumer Duty obligations.

claims.text: The chapter's rules and guidance cover how respondents should deal promptly and fairly with complaints, but the passages do not set out a full list of the complaints procedures a firm must have.

The summary details of a respondent's internal complaints handling procedures should cover at least how it fulfils its obligation to handle and seek to resolve relevant complaints. Where the complaint falls within the Financial Ombudsman Service's jurisdiction, they should also say that an unresolved complaint may be referred to the Ombudsman.
A respondent must put in place appropriate management controls and take reasonable steps to ensure that, in handling complaints, it identifies and remedies any recurring or systemic problems.

Examples of how to do this are analysing the causes of individual complaints to find common root causes, considering whether those root causes may affect other processes or products (including ones not complained of), and correcting root causes where reasonable.

Where a firm identifies recurring or systemic problems, it should consider whether to act for customers who may have suffered detriment but have not complained. If so, it should take appropriate and proportionate measures to ensure they are given appropriate redress or a proper opportunity to obtain it.

In doing so, the firm should ascertain the scope and severity of the possible consumer detriment. It should also consider whether it is fair and reasonable to undertake a proactive redress or remediation exercise, which may include contacting customers who have not complained.

If a firm identifies, through complaints, internal monitoring or any other source, that retail customers have suffered foreseeable harm from its acts or omissions, it must act in good faith and take appropriate action to rectify the situation, including providing redress where appropriate.

claims.text: Subject to DISP 1.6.2AR (which covers EMD and PSD complaints), the respondent must, by the end of eight weeks after receiving the complaint, send the complainant either a 'final response' or a written response under DISP 1.6.2R(2).

A 'final response' is a written response that accepts the complaint (offering redress or remedial action where appropriate), or offers redress or remedial action without accepting the complaint, or rejects the complaint and gives reasons. It must also enclose a copy of the Financial Ombudsman Service's standard explanatory leaflet, provide the FOS website address, inform the complainant that if still dissatisfied they may now refer the complaint to the FOS, and indicate whether the respondent consents to waive the relevant time limits in DISP 2.8.2R or DISP 2.8.7R.

Alternatively, the respondent may send a written response that explains why it is not in a position to make a final response and indicates when it expects to be able to provide one, informs the complainant that they may now refer the complaint to the FOS, indicates whether the respondent consents to waive the relevant time limits if the complaint is made or referred outside them, encloses a copy of the FOS standard explanatory leaflet, and provides the FOS website address.

raw: {"refusal": null, "claims": [{"text": "A firm must design and deliver customer support so that retail customers do not face unreasonable barriers (including unreasonable additional costs) during the lifecycle of a product, including when they want to cancel a contract, agreement or arrangement or otherwise terminate their relationship with the firm.", "cites": ["PRIN 2A.6.2"]}, {"text": "Unreasonable barriers include steps that are unreasonably onerous or time consuming, complex for a retail customer to carry out, or difficult for a retail customer to understand, and also asking retail customers for unnecessary information or evidence.", "cites": ["PRIN 2A.6.3"]}, {"text": "Unreasonable additional costs include unreasonable exit fees or other charges, delays, distress or inconvenience.", "cites": ["PRIN 2A.6.3"]}, {"text": "A firm would be unlikely to meet its obligations if its support causes or is likely to cause unreasonable delays when customers engage with it, including disproportionately longer call waiting times to cancel or make changes to an existing product than to purchase a new product.", "cites": ["PRIN 2A.6.4"]}, {"text": "A firm would also be unlikely to meet its obligations if its support causes or is likely to cause unreasonable delays to the firm requesting necessary information or evidence from customers, or to processing information or evidence received from them.", "cites": ["PRIN 2A.6.4"]}, {"text": "Appropriate friction that a firm includes in its customer journeys to mitigate the risk of harm and give customers sufficient opportunity to understand and assess their options does not amount to an unreasonable barrier.", "cites": ["PRIN 2A.6.2", "PRIN 2A.6.3"]}]}

claims.text: A firm must design and deliver customer support so that retail customers do not face unreasonable barriers (including unreasonable additional costs) during the lifecycle of a product, including when they want to cancel a contract, agreement or arrangement or otherwise terminate their relationship with the firm.

Unreasonable barriers include steps that are unreasonably onerous or time consuming, complex for a retail customer to carry out, or difficult for a retail customer to understand, and also asking retail customers for unnecessary information or evidence.
Unreasonable additional costs include unreasonable exit fees or other charges, delays, distress or inconvenience.

A firm would be unlikely to meet its obligations if its support causes or is likely to cause unreasonable delays when customers engage with it, including disproportionately longer call waiting times to cancel or make changes to an existing product than to purchase a new product.

A firm would also be unlikely to meet its obligations if its support causes or is likely to cause unreasonable delays to the firm requesting necessary information or evidence from customers, or to processing information or evidence received from them.

Appropriate friction that a firm includes in its customer journeys to mitigate the risk of harm and give customers sufficient opportunity to understand and assess their options does not amount to an unreasonable barrier.
